transcript.text: My indesit washing machine fills with water and drains but the drum just doesn't go round at all. Its an IWC something. Had it about 9 years. Is it worth fixing?

It can be worth fixing at nine years old, but it depends on which side of the drive has failed. A slipped/snapped drive belt, or worn motor brushes on an older belt-driven machine, is often a sensible repair. A seized drum/bearing, failed motor or control board can be expensive enough that replacement becomes the better option. The main possibilities are a drive belt fault, motor/brush wear or a motor-control fault; less commonly, something is physically jamming the drum. 1. Switch it off at the socket and unplug it. With the drum empty, turn it slowly by hand. Smooth and free points towards the belt or motor drive. Stiff, rough, scraping or only turning part-way points towards a trapped object or bearing problem.
2. On a short wash programme, listen from outside only: does it hum/whirr as though a motor is running while the drum remains still? That strongly favours a belt issue on a belt-driven machine. No motor sound at all makes brushes, motor control or wiring more likely. Tell me those two results and I can give a much better view of the likely repair and whether it is economically worthwhile.

I've turned it off and unplugged it, and the drum turns freely by hand, quietly, with no scraping or rumble. On a wash I can hear the relays clicking but there's no sound from a motor at all. I also noticed a faint hot electrical smell a few weeks ago, but not since.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. With relay clicks but no motor noise, plus the earlier hot electrical smell, this is more likely an electrical fault in the motor-drive circuit than simply a slipped belt. The leading possibilities are worn carbon brushes or a motor thermal cut-out on an older brushed motor; next are a burnt/loose motor connection or a motor-control board fault. A belt fault is less likely because there would usually still be some motor sound while the drum stayed still. Do not use the machine again until a qualified engineer has checked it. Ask them to inspect the motor brushes (if this version has a brushed motor), motor wiring/connectors for heat damage, the motor itself and the motor-control board, as well as confirming the belt condition. It can still be worth repairing if it proves to be brushes, a connector or a belt. If the motor-control board and motor are both damaged, at around nine years old the repair cost may make replacement the more sensible option.
